title: Ancient Greek Religion
summary: Ancient Greek religion was a polytheistic system of worship centered on the Olympian gods and countless local deities, heroes, and spirits. Unlike modern organized religions, it had no single sacred text, founding prophet, or central authority — belief and practice varied by city-state, and religious life was woven directly into civic, domestic, and agricultural life rather than kept separate from it.

key_aspects.title: Worship and sacrifice
key_aspects.description: Worship centered on maintaining good relations with the gods through prayer, votive offerings, and animal sacrifice performed at altars, usually located outside temples rather than inside them. A typical sacrifice involved burning the bones and fat for the gods while the meat was cooked and shared among worshippers — a practice that combined religious devotion with communal feasting.

key_aspects.title: Temples and priesthood
key_aspects.description: Temples served as the house of a god's cult statue rather than a congregational worship space — public rituals happened at outdoor altars nearby. Priesthood was usually a civic role rather than a full-time vocation: priests and priestesses were often prominent citizens elected or appointed for a term, responsible for maintaining a specific temple and overseeing its rites, not spiritual leaders of a wider community in the modern sense.

key_aspects.title: Oracles and divination
key_aspects.description: Greeks regularly sought divine guidance through oracles, the most famous being the Oracle of Delphi, where a priestess called the Pythia delivered prophecies believed to come from Apollo. City-states and individuals alike consulted oracles before major decisions, from wars to colonization efforts. Other forms of divination included interpreting the flight of birds, the entrails of sacrificed animals, and dreams.

key_aspects.title: Festivals
key_aspects.description: Religious festivals structured much of the civic calendar. The Panathenaea honored Athena in Athens with athletic and musical competitions. The Eleusinian Mysteries, centered on Demeter and Persephone, were secretive initiation rites promising initiates a better fate in the afterlife. The original Olympic Games themselves began as a religious festival honoring Zeus at Olympia.

key_aspects.title: Household and local worship
key_aspects.description: Alongside the major Olympian cults, everyday religious life included household deities like Hestia (goddess of the hearth), local heroes worshipped as protective figures for a particular city or region, and countless minor nature spirits (nymphs, satyrs) tied to specific springs, groves, and mountains.

key_aspects.title: Mystery cults
key_aspects.description: Alongside public civic worship, Greeks could seek out mystery cults — voluntary initiation rites promising initiates deeper religious knowledge and a better fate after death, kept deliberately secret from outsiders. The Eleusinian Mysteries, centered on Demeter and Persephone near Athens, were the most prestigious and long-running. Orphic mystery traditions, associated with the mythical poet Orpheus, offered their own initiation rites and a distinct set of beliefs about the soul's fate, and influenced later Pythagorean thought.

key_aspects.title: Philosophy and religion
key_aspects.description: From the 6th century BCE onward, Greek thinkers increasingly treated religious questions philosophically as well as ritually — see the dedicated entry, 'Greek Philosophy and Religion,' for Pythagoreanism, Orphism, Stoicism, and the late-antique Neoplatonist and theurgic traditions.
